Parramatta High School · PDHPE Depth Study Task 3

The Lookout Program

A whole-school program for youth mental health, from Year 5 to Year 12.

By Srihari, Keerti and Tanay

From Year 5 to Year 12.
Ages 10 to 19.

A universal, whole-school program for adolescents and young adults, delivered in every school. Senior students link directly to headspace, which supports people until age 25. National data is reported by age band, so the closest bands are shown.

31.8% of deaths among 15-17 year olds were suicide, up from 16.5% and 23.9% in 2001. Suicide is the leading cause of death for ages 15-24.
41 → 56 female self-harm hospitalisations per 100,000, from 2019-20 to 2023-24.
2.9% → 5% of 12-17 year olds with major depressive disorder, from 1998 to 2013-14, on the parent-reported measure the two surveys share.

Risk is measurable before 15; measuring at 15 misses the years it first appears. Among children 14 and under, suicide accounts for 2% of deaths.

Depression is common. Treatable. Not a personal failing.

Treating depression as if it were rare stops people from getting support early, when it helps most.

11% of 11-17 year olds meet the criteria for major depressive disorder. Higher than the 5% trend figure because it counts what young people report about themselves, not parent reports alone.
2nd most urgent national issue, as ranked by young Australians.

Help-seeking is a skill. Support is shared.

A learned skill, not an admission of weakness

Fewer than 25% of adolescents seek support when they need it. The program teaches the behaviours of asking: who to approach, what to say, and what happens next.

Responding to a friend is a shared responsibility

Young people often hide distress from the people who know them: parents and teachers. Peers learn to notice, check in, and connect a friend to an adult or a service.

Sequenced, interactive,
and whole-school.

Structured discussion and role-play, embedded in the curriculum. A NSW Department of Education review of 5,611 records found universal, whole-school programs with age-specific content are the most effective.

Years 5-6

Emotional literacy, recognising persistent low mood, and how to seek help. No suicide content at this stage.

Years 7-9

Symptoms, causes and treatment. Coping strategies. Noticing distress in a peer and responding.

Years 10-12

Explicit suicide prevention. Connection to headspace and other services.

There is no stand-alone solution

The Resourceful Adolescent Program and Resilient Families, both stand-alone, did not reduce depression. Whole-school delivery is what works.

YAM: suicide attempts at 12 months, 11,110 students across ten countries, trialled in Australian schools. We embed that approach whole-school.

Inside the PDHPE curriculum. No extra timetable.

Delivered through existing health and physical education classes, supported by school counsellors. NSW government schools first, then private schools, then a national rollout under the National Suicide Prevention Strategy.

Mindframe-aligned

Minimise detail about method and location. 24/7 support information is always included.

Trained teachers

Every teacher is approved or taught the basics. They are central to delivery and foster a more welcoming community for students who need help.

Informed parents

Notified in advance, with an opt-out alternative and wellbeing sessions for opted-out students.

Evaluated yearly

Results reviewed every 12 months. Only 9 of 26 programs showed sustained efficacy that far out.

Everyone finishes with a name and a number.

Act early, at the first persistent change in mood, before a more serious issue develops. Every student names one trusted adult and one service they can contact, for themselves or a friend. In-school pathways come first:

Student Support Officer Year Adviser Head Teacher Wellbeing
128,998 contacts to Kids Helpline in 2025, and 71% came outside business hours. The program teaches students to use in-school pathways and 24/7 services together, so every hour is covered.

Free, 24/7, and there when school isn't.

We teach every student that help exists outside school hours: who answers, what they offer, and how to call. No student leaves without the numbers.

Kids Helpline1800 55 1800Free 24/7 counselling, ages 5-25
Lifeline13 11 1424-hour crisis support
eheadspace1800 650 890Online and phone support, ages 12-25, plus headspace centres

QLife1800 184 527LGBTIQ+ peer support
000In an emergency, call 000.

Resilience is a set of practised skills.

The most effective programs are strength-based: they build on what students already do well, rather than relying on cognitive behavioural training alone. Each tier practises its own skills.

Skills by stage

Years 5-6: emotional regulation
Years 7-9: stress management and coping
Years 10-12: safe peer response

The wellbeing plan

Every student keeps a personal plan:

Their warning signs
Two coping strategies: sleep routine, exercise, grounding
One trusted adult, and one service they can call, for themselves or a friend

Notice it. Name it. Say something.

Depression is common, treatable, and never a personal failing. Help-seeking is a skill, and skills are taught. Here is what our program asks of every student.

  • For yourself. If your mood has been low for more than two weeks, tell your one trusted adult. Early is easier.
  • For a friend. Ask them directly, listen, and don't keep it secret. Take them to an adult.
  • Before you leave today. Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800. Free, 24/7.
